extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, agency counsel, environmental/regulatory lawyers, and courts reviewing the rule
extracted.subtask_description: A legal-administrative-comment arguing that EPA's proposed repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding is unlawful. Focuses on application of the major-questions doctrine, binding precedent (Massachusetts v. EPA), and APA standards for reasoned decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The major-questions doctrine applies in 'extraordinary cases' where an agency asserts highly consequential power beyond what Congress could reasonably be understood to have granted. The core inquiry asks whether the novelty and breadth of the asserted regulatory power provide reason to doubt that Congress intended to implicitly delegate that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors drawn from Brown & Williamson, West Virginia, and UARG include: whether the assertion is 'unheralded' (novel), whether it is a 'transformative expansion' of agency authority, and whether it has profound economic and political significance. Courts look to the history and breadth of the asserted authority, economic and political significance, the vintage of the assertion, whether Congress' past actions suggest it reserved the issue for itself, and the clarity with which Congress spoke to the agency's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massachusetts v. EPA controls on Section 202(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Massachusetts concluded the Clean Air Act 'unambiguously' authorized EPA to regulate greenhouse gases under Section 202(a) and rejected EPA's reliance on Brown & Williamson to avoid that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is bound by Massachusetts' holding that (1) Section 202(a) authorizes greenhouse-gas regulation and (2) recognizing that authority did not implicate the major-questions doctrine. Any final action premised on the belief that Massachusetts' major-questions analysis is no longer good law would itself be unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must explain departures from prior positions (Fox/Arbitrary-and-Capricious)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency departs from a prior position, it must acknowledge and provide a reasoned explanation for the change; failure to do so renders final agency action arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final rule failing to acknowledge and explain departures between the new approach and the agency's prior, detailed analyses (including recent multi-pollutant standards and multi-page responses to comments) would be arbitrary and capricious. See Fox and State Farm principles requiring reasoned explanation of changed positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Farm/APA requirement to consider important aspects and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Under State Farm and general APA arbitrariness review, an agency must consider and address important aspects of the problem and cannot ignore alternatives or relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot rely on a flawed framing of the interpretive question or ignore evidence of other available control technologies; if EPA claims the major-questions doctrine bars Section 202(a) it must show that every available means of regulating greenhouse gases under that section would be barred. Failing to consider such aspects or to respond to countervailing evidence renders the action arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: UARG economic-impact criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: UARG applied the major-questions lens where applying statutory text would dramatically expand the number of regulated sources and impose massive economic and administrative burdens (e.g., PSD permit applications increasing from ~800 to ~82,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed regulatory interpretation raises major-questions concerns if it would increase the universe of regulated entities by orders of magnitude, require rewriting statutory thresholds to make the statute functional, or impose vast administrative and economic costs inconsistent with Congressional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: West Virginia transformative-regulation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: West Virginia found the major-questions doctrine implicated where EPA used a provision to mandate systemwide shifts in an industry (e.g., changing how electricity is generated) rather than traditional source-by-source pollution-control measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major-questions concerns arise where the regulation (a) mandates wholesale shifting of an industry, (b) requires the agency to make decisions outside its typical technical expertise (transmission, distribution, storage), or (c) effectively substitutes a program Congress considered and rejected (e.g., cap-and-trade). Distinguish technology-based emissions standards that improve individual source performance from systemwide mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unheralded/vintage-of-assertion inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts assess whether the authority was 'unheralded' at the time asserted or has been consistently exercised; long, consistent exercise reduces a finding that the claim is an unheralded major question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPA has regulated greenhouse gases under Section 202(a) for 15+ years, with repeated rulemakings and no rebuke from Congress or courts, that history cuts against treating Section 202(a) regulation as an unheralded assertion of authority. Compare timelines in Biden, NFIB, UARG, West Virginia where asserted authority was much more recently adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis and overruling precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency (or court) seeking to overturn longstanding statutory-interpretation precedent must grapple with stare decisis factors and the presumption against overruling decisions of statutory interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposal to rely on a new major-questions analysis that would effectively overturn Massachusetts must address the stare decisis considerations the Supreme Court uses when deciding whether to overrule precedent; failure to do so undermines the lawfulness of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate characterization of regulatory effects (EV 'mandate' issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must accurately describe the nature and effects of its prior regulations; mischaracterizing prior standards (e.g., labeling them an 'electric vehicle mandate') is improper and unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposal wrongly characterizes prior greenhouse-gas standards as an EV mandate. The Agency must show factual linkage between the endangerment finding and later regulations if it claims those regulations demonstrate a transformation beyond what Massachusetts contemplated; unsupported factual claims or mischaracterizations undercut reliance on major-questions reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-text/clear congressional authorization standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the major-questions doctrine is implicated, the statute's plain text (i.e., clear congressional authorization) can overcome the doctrinal hesitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the statutory language unambiguously authorizes the agency's action (as Massachusetts found for Section 202(a)), the major-questions doctrine does not bar the regulation. Agency must demonstrate lack of clear congressional authorization before invoking major-questions to limit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show blanket invalidation of Section 202(a) applications
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify repealing the 2009 endangerment finding on major-questions grounds, EPA would need to show that the doctrine bars regulation of greenhouse gases under Section 202(a) in all possible applications—not merely some means of regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough to argue certain methods (e.g., particular electrification-focused measures) might offend the major-questions doctrine; EPA must demonstrate that every application of Section 202(a) would violate the doctrine. Absent such a showing, wholesale repeal is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of subsequent legislation and administrative developments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency cannot rely on asserted conflicts with subsequent congressional or administrative actions without correctly analyzing whether those developments actually undercut prior precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's invocation of later legislation or actions to argue Massachusetts is undermined is incorrect unless it shows a real conflict; the agency must explain why intervening legislation or its own later practices legitimately alter the earlier major-questions analysis.
